questions.q: What does the cited Gidney & Ekerå (2019) estimate claim about factoring RSA-2048 with Shor's algorithm on a surface-code architecture?
options: It has already been successfully run on current hardware
It would require no error correction at all
It would require exactly 7 physical qubits, matching the Steane code
It would require on the order of 20 million physical qubits, running for roughly 8 hours
questions.explain: This is presented in the lesson explicitly as a widely cited published literature estimate, not something derived from the lesson's own arithmetic.

questions.q: In the lesson's own worked example, how many physical qubits are needed for 100 logical qubits each protected at d=15 (449 physical qubits per logical qubit)?
questions.explain: 100 x 449 = 44,900, a directly computed illustrative example distinct from the cited literature figure.

questions.q: Why does the lesson insist on keeping the cited Gidney & Ekerå figure and the illustrative 44,900-qubit example clearly separate?
options: There is no real reason to distinguish them; either number can be used interchangeably

The cited figure reflects a detailed analysis of an actual algorithm's real circuit structure and overheads (like magic-state distillation), while the illustrative example is a simplified multiplication meant only to show the method
They are actually the same number, just rounded differently
The illustrative example is more accurate than the cited literature figure
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly separates a literature citation (grounded in real algorithm analysis) from its own simplified worked arithmetic, to avoid conflating a precise published result with an illustrative teaching example.

questions.q: What core multiplication does the lesson's illustrative estimate use, and why does it still matter despite being simplified?
options: (physical qubits per logical qubit) x (number of logical qubits needed) -- the first-order building block that more detailed estimates, including the cited literature figure, build upon
(number of classical bits) x (number of ancilla qubits), a formula not used anywhere else in the course
There is no meaningful multiplication involved; the number was simply asserted
(code distance) x (number of rounds of syndrome extraction), unrelated to qubit count
questions.explain: The simple multiplication of per-logical-qubit cost by number of logical qubits is the dominant first-order term that any fuller resource estimate, including published ones, starts from.

questions.q: What is the lesson's honest bottom-line comparison between these resource estimates and current NISQ-era hardware?
options: Both the cited ~20 million qubit estimate and the illustrative 44,900 qubit example are vastly larger than anything current hardware (tens to low hundreds of noisy qubits) can run
The cited estimate has already been achieved by current quantum computers
Current hardware can already comfortably run algorithms requiring 44,900 physical qubits
NISQ-era hardware has no qubit count limitations relevant to this comparison
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that both figures dwarf current NISQ-era qubit counts, reinforcing the course's honesty requirement that useful-scale fault tolerance remains a forward-looking goal.
